To ease the transition, the CiscoSecurityCloud 3.x branch will be actively maintained and should remain the recommended stable branch for customers who require the existing FTD sourcetype behavior. item.title: Cyberwatch Syslog Add-on for Splunk - v2.0.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
### Version 2.0.0 This is a major release. **It changes the value of every field this add-on produces.** Read the breaking changes below before upgrading if you have searches, alerts or dashboards built on version 1.0.x. #### Breaking changes **Field values no longer carry quotes.** **Timestamps are now extracted.** **Three fields are removed.** `description` and `name` were both copies of `cve_code` — use `cve` and `signature`. `severity_id` held the string `level_high` in a field the CIM types as a number — use `severity`. **`cvss_vector` is now the vendor's own.** 1.0.3 overwrote it with a CVSS v2 vector rebuilt from `cvss_AV`, `cvss_AC` and `cvss_Au.`Cyberwatch sends a complete, versioned vector of its own (`CVSS:3.1/...`, `CVSS:4.0/...`), and that is what you now get. #### Added * **All 24 fields Cyberwatch emits are extracted and documented** — `epss`, `triage_status`, `computer_criticality`, `computer_os_name`, `computer_os_arch`, `computer_category`, `computer_id`, `groups`, `active`, `ignored`, `fixed_at`, `created_at`, `updated_at` and `source_node` were never usable before. * **CIM mapping reviewed against the Vulnerabilities data model, CIM 8.x.** `cvss` is converted to a number, and `severity` is mapped explicitly from `cve_level`. When Cyberwatch reports `level_unknown`, `severity` is left unset: the CIM prescribes `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` and `informational`, none of which means "the source does not know". * **An explicit time zone.** The BSD syslog header carries none, so the add-on declares `TZ = UTC` — every timestamp in the Cyberwatch payload is UTC. Override it in local/props.conf if your appliance emits local time. * Line breaking, truncation and event breaker settings are declared. #### Changed * The `cyberwatch_vulnerability_detection` event type now keys on the extracted `cve_code` field instead of matching the literal string `CVE-` anywhere in the event, which tagged any message merely mentioning an identifier. #### Upgrading 1. Install 2.0.0 over the existing add-on. Your `local/` directory is preserved, so your input configuration survives. 2. **Restart Splunk.** The timestamp and line-breaking settings are index-time settings and do not apply until you do. 3. Update any search that compares field values against the quoted form. #### Compatibility Splunk Enterprise 8.0 and later, Splunk Cloud Platform. No Python, no scripted inputs, no custom UI.


Description:
The Cyberwatch Syslog Add-on for Splunk allows a Splunk software administrator to collect data in syslog format from Cyberwatch. This add-on provides the inputs and CIM-compatible knowledge to use with other Splunk apps, such as Splunk Enterprise Security.

item.title: Spaces Add-On for Splunk - v2.0.11 [Version Update]

Release Notes:
This maintenance release fixes Cisco Spaces Firehose authorization recovery and improves the operator experience. * Preserves the Meta Streams account configuration when Cisco Spaces returns an HTTP 401 response. * Attempts one automatic refresh of a rejected cached API key using the configured Activation Token. * Keeps the account intact and reports an actionable error when automatic recovery fails. * Improves Collection Health troubleshooting for recovered, pending, failed, and unresolved authorization states. * Adds direct navigation to Home, Connections, Data Collection, Collection Health, and Search. * Displays the installed add-on version and build number on Home. * Updates runtime dependencies and strengthens release-package validation. After upgrading, replace the Activation Token only if automatic recovery fails and Cisco Spaces continues to reject the credentials.


Short Description:
The Spaces Add-on for Splunk enables ingestion of location intelligence and occupancy data from Cisco Spaces into Splunk. The add-on connects to Cisco Spaces APIs and collects device presence, engagement, and space analytics data, making it searchable and actionable within Splunk.


Description:
The Spaces Add-on for Splunk enables the ingestion of location analytics, occupancy insights, device telemetry, and engagement data from Cisco Spaces into Splunk. Organizations leveraging Cisco Spaces for indoor location intelligence, presence analytics, and asset visibility often need to operationalize that data within broader security, IT, facilities, or business analytics workflows. This add-on provides a secure and configurable integration that collects data from Cisco Spaces APIs and normalizes it for use within Splunk. By bringing Cisco Spaces data into Splunk, organizations can: Correlate physical space utilization with IT and security events Monitor occupancy and device presence trends Enhance operational visibility across facilities and campus environments Support analytics, dashboards, and alerting use cases within Splunk The add-on uses modular inputs to retrieve data from Cisco Spaces and leverages Splunk’s credential storage for secure authentication handling. This add-on is designed for customers who want to extend the value of Cisco Spaces data into their Splunk environment for search, correlation, visualization, and operational intelligence use cases.

Release Notes:
# spiderSilk Resonance Add-On for Splunk — Version 1.3.0 ## Before you upgrade **This release requires Splunk 9.3.0 or later.** Support for Splunk 9.0.x – 9.2.x has been withdrawn. Those versions ship Python 3.7, which the libraries this add-on depends on no longer support. If you run Splunk 9.2 or earlier, please stay on version 1.2.0 until you are able to upgrade Splunk. Supported and tested: **9.3.x, 9.4.x, 10.0.x** ## Fixed **Data ingestion could stop permanently and never restart.** If a crawl was interrupted part-way through — a Splunk restart, a network timeout, or the process being killed — the add-on could be left holding a run lock it was unable to clear. Every later run then exited immediately, and ingestion stopped silently for threats, dark web leakages and assets alike. No error was surfaced in the add-on's dashboard. Upgrading resolves this automatically: the first run after the upgrade clears the stale lock and resumes crawling. No manual cleanup is required. If you were affected, threats and leakages that were created *and* closed during the outage were never indexed and cannot be recovered. Everything still open at the time of upgrade will be ingested on the next crawl. **Event timestamps were unreliable.** Two problems, both corrected: * Splunk was choosing the timestamp automatically and could pick a different date field as the payload changed shape. Each data type now uses a fixed field — threats use the creation date, dark web leakages the date the leakage was recorded, and assets the date they last changed. * Timestamps from the Resonance API are in UTC, but were being read in the Splunk server's local time zone. On a server set to UTC+3 this placed every event three hours away from its true time. These corrections apply to newly indexed events. Events already in your index keep the timestamps they were given when indexed. ## Improved * **The add-on package is around 70% smaller** (roughly 18 MB down to 5 MB), which makes distribution and search head deployment noticeably faster. * Bundled third-party libraries have been updated to current versions. * Network requests to the Resonance API now wait longer before timing out, which reduces failed crawls on large data sets and slower connections. ## Good to know Events are timestamped with the **date on the record itself** — when a threat was created, or when an asset last changed — rather than the time the add-on collected it. A threat raised some time ago but collected today will appear at its original creation date, not at today's date. This means a search over "Last 24 hours" shows recent *threats*, not recent *ingestion*. To confirm the add-on is collecting data, search by index time instead: ``` index= sourcetype=resonance_* earliest=0 | stats count, max(_indextime) AS last_collected BY sourcetype | convert ctime(last_collected) ``` ## Support Questions or issues: [info@spidersilk.com](mailto:info@spidersilk.com)

Release Notes:
\# Inno Observability 1.3.1 \## Highlights \*\*Guided agent deployment.\*\* The Agent Deploy screen now walks you through the whole path — what to enter, what is already decided, what is optional — and generates a command you can copy and run as-is. Install, verify, and uninstall are one line each. \*\*Central management via a Splunk deployment server.\*\* Install the Universal Forwarder on a target server once; the collector and its configuration come from the deployment server after that. Version and settings changes are then made in Splunk alone, without touching the monitored servers. \*\*Per-application APM instrumentation.\*\* Java instrumentation now attaches to one application at a time instead of the whole host. Applications that already have another APM agent are detected and skipped, so several applications can share a server safely. Applying it does not restart your application — you choose when to restart. \*\*Works without internet.\*\* The instrumentation library ships with the app, so servers in a closed network fetch it from your Splunk instance. No staging step, no per-server file copying. \*\*Clustered services.\*\* Give every node the same service name and they appear as one service with one instance per server, so you can compare throughput, error rate and latency across instances and see which node is at fault. The same applies to databases, message brokers and caches through a new solution cluster name. \## Fixes \- \`--dry-run\` no longer installs anything when the deployment server method is used. It previously ran the real installation while reporting a preview. \- \`--uninstall\` now removes the Universal Forwarder and the instrumentation library. It previously reported success while leaving the forwarder running. \- Commands that still contain placeholders (\`\\`, \`\\`) are rejected with a message naming the field to fill in. They were previously installed as-is, which sent data to an unusable address without any error. \- Instrumentation targets are addressed by unit name. Target numbers could change when a JVM restarted, which could apply or remove instrumentation on the wrong application. \- Host names are attached to metrics on the deployment-server path, so infrastructure screens and agent status join correctly. \- Solution receivers and tags are no longer offered where they have no effect; the screen says why and what to do instead. \- Valid licences are accepted on search head clusters and other licence peers, where the deployment ID could previously be read as empty. \## Notes \- Korean, English and Japanese interfaces. \- No licence key is included. Without a key the app runs in demonstration mode. \- Requires a Splunk deployment server for the central-management method; single-server installation is available as an alternative.

Inno Observability turns OpenTelemetry spans in your Splunk indexes into ready-made APM dashboards — service and endpoint response times, error rates, trace search and a span waterfall, plus Kubernetes and host context for the same time window. It reads data you already collect and runs entirely inside your own Splunk deployment.

item.title: Adjutant AI (AI Workbench) - v2.5.9 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-09-10 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.5.8**: playbooks that carry all of their instructions, and every path to an AI service agreeing about where a request goes. **2.5.9** is in development and adds nothing yet. 2.5.8 sits on top of **2.5.4**'s readable RCA report and **2.5.3**'s private LLM endpoints and **2.5.2**'s one connection for several tenants and **2.5.1**'s fixes to **2.5.0**'s setup wizard and **2.4.2** — a data-correctness fix on top of **2.4.1**, a connectivity release on top of the **2.4.0** integration workstream and **2.2.2**, itself a maintenance release on **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.5.9 (in development) **2.5.8 is the current published release**, and its notes below are exactly what shipped. ### Which model you are actually talking to From a customer on Azure OpenAI behind a gateway, reporting that 2.5.8 changed nothing about model detection. They were right, and the reason is worth separating into two halves. **Discovering a model list genuinely is impossible on their endpoint.** Their gateway does not forward the route that lists models and answers 404, so there is no list to read. "Does not apply" was the correct verdict. What made it read as a fault of ours is that the row showed the bare 404 next to it and no reason, so a property of their gateway looked like a gap in the product. The row now says the endpoint publishes no model list. **But the run had already learned the model and was throwing it away.** The check below it asks a real question, and the reply names the model that answered it. That is the only way a gateway-fronted resource ever reveals what is behind a deployment, and the screen showed a duration. It now names it: *answered as gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14*. **And the model field can disagree with what replied.** On an Azure address that names a deployment, the deployment decides which model runs, so the model field never reaches the provider and a wrong value there cannot fail any check. It is not decorative, though: it is the name your usage and spend are recorded under. A connection running gpt-4.1-mini while configured as gpt-4o-mini is billed correctly by Microsoft and reported wrongly by us. The wizard now says so before you save, and names the value to use. A deployment name in that field is still not treated as a disagreement, because a deployment name and a model name are not comparable and warning about it would fire on every healthy Azure resource. **Both list routes are now asked before we conclude there is none.** Azure documents two, and the address does not tell you which a resource serves: the dated `/openai/models?api-version=`, and `/openai/v1/models`, which Microsoft now documents as the model list operation. A gateway publishes whichever its author implemented, and forwarding one says nothing about the other. We asked one, and reported that the endpoint published no list on the strength of it. Both are asked now, and the check names the routes it tried, so the statement can be checked rather than taken on trust. If your gateway does publish the other one, discovery simply works. Worth knowing even when the list is readable: it returns your **account's model catalogue**, which can run to hundreds of entries, not the deployments on this resource and not the model behind the one you are calling. Mapping a deployment to its model needs the Azure control plane, which takes an Entra token and subscription permissions rather than the inference key. So on a gateway-fronted resource the completion response is not a second-best source for which model you are getting. It is the only one that credential can reach. **The support package carries the routes**, so a failed run records which questions were asked and not only the verdict. Adding them meant URLs entering the evidence section, which was copied field by field with no URL redaction of its own -- redaction ran on the request and the configuration. Evidence URLs are now redacted by shape rather than by field name, so an endpoint pasted as `https://user:pass@host/...` cannot carry its credential into the file, and a URL field added later is covered without anyone having to remember. --- ## 2.5.8 "Everything it was told to do" Two customers and a day of reading what the product actually sent, rather than what it was meant to send. Most of what follows was found by opening a diagnostic package and comparing the two. ### Playbooks were running without most of their instructions **This affected every playbook run from the Ask tab, and it is the reason to take this release.** A playbook is a short procedure plus a set of reusable **skills** it declares: the rules on correctness traps, performance priorities, evidence, naming, and so on. Picking a playbook from the Ask screen sent the procedure and none of the skills. It was invisible from either end. A playbook declaring nine skills produced a prompt byte for byte identical to one declaring none, and nothing reported a skill as missing. On "Improve an existing SPL" that meant 7,536 characters were sent where 40,469 were intended. Five sixths of its instructions were absent. It surfaced as a review that was thinner than it should have been. A customer asked it to improve `index=* NOT index=_* | stats c by sourcetype` and it never mentioned `tstats`, which is the standard way to make exactly that search faster and is written down in the very skill that was not being sent. Playbooks reached through the assistant's own router were unaffected, which is why this survived testing. If a playbook has ever given you a shallower answer than you expected, it is worth running again. ### A dashboard reported as created that was never created The result panel would say "Created dashboard", show a green "Validation: OK" and offer a link that returned 404. The dashboard that existed, and rendered correctly once you found it, was under an internal staging name. Publishing writes to a staging name first and promotes it only after the rendered dashboard has been checked, so that a dashboard which fails that check never exists at its real name. That part was right. What was wrong is that a failure to promote still reported success, under the name the dashboard would have had. Worse, the staged copy is on a short lease, so the working dashboard was going to be cleaned up on its own. Two separate paths did this and both are fixed. A publish that does not complete now says so, names the staged copy and links to it so you can see what the check saw, and no longer produces a link to something that is not there. ### Connecting to an AI service: one story, several causes **This is the reason to take the release.** A customer set up Azure OpenAI behind a gateway, watched the wizard report 8 of 8, and could not ask a question. That happened more than once, and each time the cause was different, so it is worth saying what they had in common rather than listing them as separate faults. The product reaches an AI service by more than one path: the setup checks, the request path through the Splunk server, the browser-direct path, and the scheduled health check. Each had grown its own answer to questions all four have to agree on, and the checks were the path that happened to be right. That is the worst possible arrangement, because the screen a customer is shown passing is not the one serving them. All four now derive the address from one place, and a test compares them across every service and every Azure address shape. It asserts they **agree** rather than asserting any one is correct: a checker that agrees with itself and disagrees with the thing it checks proves nothing. What was actually wrong: * **Gemini did not work through the Splunk server**, which is the only way it can be called. The request went to the stored address, and for Gemini that address is the model list rather than a completion. * **Azure stored as a plain resource address** went to that address instead of to the deployment. * **Azure stored as a complete address** was rebuilt into one URL carrying two deployments, which is what a gateway answered "Resource not found" to. * **A connection with no address stored could not be used at all**, returning *"LLM config has no endpoint stored"* on a connection that had just passed every check. Most services publish one fixed address and are never asked for it, so an empty field is correct, and five parts of the app each had to work the address out. Two did not. Connections you already saved now work without being re-saved. * **A new connection defaulted to being called from the browser**, and so did one whose call mode had never been recorded. That default was the wrong way round: most services refuse a browser outright, a private endpoint is not reachable from a desktop at all, and the key would have to reach the browser to even try. Three places chose it, including the form that creates connections, while the setup wizard had already moved to going through the Splunk server. All three now agree with the wizard. **A connection you already have is untouched**: its own setting always wins, so a working browser-direct connection stays browser-direct. * **A connection on a private address was marked Failed twice a day.** 2.5.3 taught the setup checks that an Azure Private Endpoint, an AWS PrivateLink interface and a gateway inside your VNet are on private addresses by construction; the scheduled check never learned it, so it refused the address the wizard had just proved. A working OpenAI or Anthropic connection hit the same thing for a different reason, and was told it had a bad URL scheme. You would have seen eight green checks and a red badge on one screen. Loopback and link-local addresses are still refused by every check, and a name that resolves to both a public and a loopback address is still refused. Those are the ones worth refusing. Also fixed: the network panel had been listing no hosts at all for services with a fixed address, so it had nothing to say about the only destination that mattered. ### The support diagnostics key has been replaced The "Report an issue" package is encrypted to a key only we hold. That key has been rotated and the previous one retired, after its private half was exposed during a support conversation. Nothing is required of you, and no diagnostics were at risk: the key protects a file **after** you choose to send it, and every package is redacted before encryption, so it never carries credentials in the first place. Packages you sent under the old key still open, because each records which key sealed it. ### Azure OpenAI behind somebody else's gateway Reported by a customer whose Azure OpenAI sits behind an Azure Function on a private endpoint. Every connection check passed, a real question came back answered, and the wizard then refused to save the connection. **The deployment name is the model name.** Azure identifies a model by the deployment named in the URL path, which is how it works whenever the service is fronted by a gateway. That surface publishes no model list, so the "finding models that work" check correctly stands aside, and Azure has no default to fall back on. The wizard ran eight live checks, got an answer out of the deployment, and then reported it had no model to save. It now reads the deployment name from the endpoint. A model you enter yourself still wins, and an endpoint that genuinely names no deployment still says so. **The final step could fail after everything else passed.** The last check assembles the configuration and touches no network, and it could still fail with an internal error on a run where everything had succeeded. The 2.4.0 reliability work rewrote the retry module in place rather than adding to it, which deleted the LLM call orchestrator — while its one caller, the proxy that **every** Ask goes through, still called it. The result was an `AttributeError` on every request, surfaced as a generic internal error with the real reason only in `splunkd.log`. The orchestrator is restored alongside the newer retry helper. The two are disjoint and stay that way: one is the writer's bounded per-request retry, the other is the provider fallback chain with its circuit breaker and per-attempt journal. `tests/test_llm_retry.py` covers the restored path and was failing on `import` for two releases, which is how this reached a release at all. ### Network-policy events were merged, not split When a device snapshot was stored to a Splunk index, every rule from that device arrived as a **single event** containing the whole batch of JSON records, instead of one event per rule. The same applied to the object, warning and snapshot families. Nothing announced it. The field list still showed `rule_id`, `action`, `source_values` and the rest, because Splunk extracts fields from the first JSON object in an event — so the fields you clicked on were real and correct. Only the **count** was wrong, and the counts the app itself reported were counts of records submitted, not of events landed. A `| stats count by device_id` over the rule source type therefore under-reported by however many rules a device had. The cause was a single character. `default/props.conf` declared the parsing rules under `[adjutant:network_policy:*]`, and props.conf applies its wildcard match language to `source::` and `host::` stanzas only — in a source-type stanza the `*` is literal, so the stanza matched nothing and the events fell back to Splunk's defaults. Each family now has its own stanza, and a `[source::itmip_llm_splunk_writer]` stanza backstops any source type added to that path in future. ### A policy field was colliding with one of Splunk's own Expanded policy tuples carry a field named `source` — and `source` is one of the fields Splunk defines on every event, where it names what wrote the record. Splunk does not overwrite on a collision, it **merges**, so `| table source` returned the policy's source address and `itmip_llm_splunk_writer` together in one cell, with nothing to say which was which. Fields whose names Splunk already owns are now written as `original_` — so that one is `original_source`. This applies to the **index** write only: the KV Store rows, the policy graph and the API keep the model's own names, because `source` is part of what a `tuple_id` is hashed from and renaming it there would move every tuple id ever issued. ### `source` and `host` said who wrote the event, not where the data came from Every network-policy event landed with `source = itmip_llm_splunk_writer` and `host = ai_workbench` — true of every event this app has ever written, and therefore no use for filtering or for a CIM-style view of where a policy came from. They now describe the input. `host` is the box the configuration was **read from**: the device or manager when it was reached over the network, and the Splunk instance itself when the input was a file or a paste, because that is the machine that held it. `source` names the input — a file path when the collector recorded one, else the file name, else `cisco:asa:config` for a device configuration or `cisco:fmc:api` for a manager collection. An FMC collection is labelled by the **manager**, not by the device platform it describes, which is the distinction the field is for. ### An Org with its own mapping collection saw an empty one — or someone else's An Org that registers a `mapping_collection` gets its own (`itmip_ai_mappings_`), which is the isolation boundary. The shipped example mappings were only ever seeded into `DFLT`'s, so that collection stayed **empty**: the examples were invisible to the Org, and an integration resolving its `mapping_ref` at run time under that Org found nothing. Compounding it, the Mappings tab did not tell the server which app it was in, so it resolved as the fallback Org and displayed **DFLT's** collection. An admin could Verify and Clear a mapping there, and a schedule running under their real Org would still refuse — pointing at a row in a collection nobody was looking at. The shipped examples are now seeded per Org, and the tab resolves the same Org the runtime does. **One consequence to know about:** mappings authored while the tab was mis-resolving live in the fallback Org's collection. They are not lost, but they belong to that Org and will not appear under yours. Re-create or re-scope anything you need. ### Seeded mappings could never be corrected after the first install A seeded mapping is documented as re-seed-eligible: ship a fix, and an untouched system-owned row picks it up. It never worked. The seeder POSTed to the KV Store collection root, which only ever **inserts** — splunkd answers `409` for a `_key` that already exists and leaves the row alone — and the 409 landed in a bare `except: pass`. Every correction to a shipped mapping since the first install was silently dropped. A second guard compounded it: the seeder skipped any row cleared for unattended use. That was added for a real reason (restarts were resetting clearance) but it froze the whole row rather than the decision, so the mapping most likely to run unattended was the one fixes could never reach. On a real instance the shipped Cisco ASA mapping was still at its pre-B3.3 shape: **no `device_id` in the projection** and **no `source.schema_version`**, so the writer's schema pin had nothing to compare and could not refuse a batch the mapping would silently strip of its NAT view. The refusal that exists to prevent exactly that could not fire. Now: the seeder replaces then inserts, so corrections land; and clearance is carried across an unchanged re-seed but **revoked when the content actually changed**, recording who had cleared it and why it was revoked. A human cleared a specific mapping, not a name — so a changed mapping stops and asks, instead of running under an approval that no longer describes it. ### The shipped ASA Playbook pointed at a superseded mapping "Cisco ASA Policy Ingestion (mapping-driven)" was wired to `cisco-asa-config-to-network-policy-v1`, which is `superseded_by` v2 and pinned to source schema 1.0. The Playbook now names v2. The trailing `-v1` / `-v2` in a mapping name is its **schema generation**, not its lifecycle version; a mapping carries its own `operational v1` separately. Two axes, one letter. The Playbook's mapping picker now shows each mapping's title alongside its ref (the Mappings tab lists them by title, so the same mapping looked like two different objects), flags a superseded choice with the successor's name before you save, and spells out that clearing for unattended is a separate step from promoting. ### Policy records were stamped with the wrong Org and BU Run a network-policy ingestion from the Ask tab in a host app such as `itmip_fis_app`, with the header showing your real Org and BU, and every landed record still said `tenant_org: DFLT`, `tenant_bu: DFLT`. The Ask request itself sends that app; the tool dispatch behind it did not, so resolution fell back to the assistant app's own name — which matches whichever Org registered *that* pattern, not the one the user is in. An Org whose `app_patterns` name the host app could never match. The netpol, `splunk_memory` and `splunk_mapping` tool calls now send the host app. This is a context hint, not a grant — an Org matches only when the caller's real roles also match its `role_patterns` — so it cannot widen anyone's access; it makes tenant data land under the tenant it belongs to. Redaction on the import path is opt-in, so unless it was asked for, a stored artifact still contains the secrets the scanner merely counted — on our own sample config, an enable-password hash and two IKEv2 pre-shared keys. No functional change: every netpol read goes through the endpoint's system token, and that endpoint was already admin-gated. One idiom now locates a warning and a rule alike. To correct history, remove the affected events and re-store the snapshots. --- ## 2.4.1 "Getting connected" Everything here came out of two customer setups in the same fortnight: an Azure OpenAI service published through a corporate API gateway, and one behind a private endpoint. The release is about closing the distance between "the test passes" and "it works", and about not making an administrator assemble a URL by hand from three values nobody gave them. ### Find my endpoint (Azure OpenAI) Azure needs the complete address of a deployment, not the address of the service: everything up to and including `/chat/completions`, with the deployment name and an api-version in it. Behind a gateway that address also carries a path prefix chosen by whoever publishes the API. An administrator is typically handed a base URL and expected to work out the other three parts, and getting any of them wrong produces a "Resource not found" that reads like a permissions problem. There is now a **Find my endpoint** button beneath the endpoint field. Give it whatever you were given — often just the hostname — and it works out the rest from the Splunk server itself, then offers to fill in the endpoint, the deployment and the api-version in one click. It finds the address by paying attention to *how* each attempt is refused rather than just that it failed. A gateway refusing an address it does not publish answers differently from Azure refusing a deployment name it does not have, and the second kind of refusal proves the rest of the address is already right. The licence page now says the key was issued without a device limit and needs reissuing, instead of sending administrators round a loop that had no exit. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. It will not decline a card payment in a hundred milliseconds; that is what the dedicated engines are for. It is the layer above them that finds what they miss across channels, connects the entities they cannot, and turns three weeks of investigation into an afternoon with a trail you can hand to an auditor. ## 2.0.7 "Memory, Scheduled Ask & Integrations" Adjutant AI gains a durable memory, a scheduled/unattended surface, and a governed data-integration subsystem — so it stops re-asking, can run on a clock, and can sync a system of record into Splunk under a contract two humans have reviewed. - **Memory — it stops re-asking.** A small, durable, per-tenant memory: **learned facts** (the index a report uses, what "the Cribl search" means for a team) captured the moment they're learned, and **integration watermarks**. See `docs/ADJUTANT_MEMORY_AND_SCHEDULED_ASK.md` for the operator guide. ## 2.0.6 "ITSI RCA — Industrialise" The Root Cause Analysis engine reaches its industrialise milestone, and the smaller items deferred from earlier trains are completed. If you set either in a local override, update it. --- ## 1.8.5 "CIM Coverage Audit" When a data source is onboarded but a correlation search in Enterprise Security still comes back empty, or an ITSI KPI never fills, the cause is almost always that the source is not properly mapped to the CIM data model the search depends on. Finding out why is normally a slow, manual walk through the layers. The CIM Coverage Audit does it for you, from your real events and your real search head configuration. **New** - **Audit a sourcetype against a CIM dataset.** Ask, for example, audit cisco:asa against the Network Traffic All_Traffic dataset. You get back how much of the dataset the source covers, and if it does not, which layer is broken: the source is not tagged so the model cannot see it, its index is not on the model's allowlist, a field is missing or under the wrong name, a value needs normalizing, or the accelerated summaries the correlation searches read have not caught up. That last one is the confusing case where CIM works when you test it by hand but your correlation searches fire nothing, and the audit calls it out plainly. - **A fix you can read and deploy.** For each gap the audit produces the exact configuration, checked for validity, shown as your current stanza next to the proposed one, with a note on where it belongs. It never deploys anything itself. You review and apply it, which is what lets you run this where an automatic write to production would never pass change control. - **Honest about what a search head can see.** Adjutant AI runs on the search head, so it reads your search time configuration and the real events, and it is upfront that it cannot read the index time configuration on your indexers. It runs its searches as you, so it can never read data from an index you could not otherwise search. - Three read only helpers to read a sourcetype's search head props and transforms and check where a sourcetype has data. The diagnosis is available on Professional so any platform team can see which layer is broken. Generating the validated fix is an Enterprise feature. It grades against the CIM add on actually installed on your search head. Restart Splunk after upgrading. **Fixed** - **The app opens on the Ask tab again.** If your LLM runs entirely on the search head, with the key held server side (the Splunk proxy mode, an Azure managed identity, or a Bedrock role), the browser never receives an API key. The app used to read that as nothing being configured and jumped to the Settings tab on every launch. It now opens on Ask as intended, and only sends you to Settings when a key really is needed and missing. - **Clearer license status.** When a license is installed but the app cannot confirm it is active on this environment, it now tells you that directly instead of quietly dropping to the free Personal tier. Admins get a pointer to the License page to re-activate. --- ## 1.8.4 "Async playbooks over MCP" Run Adjutant AI playbooks from an AI agent over the Model Context Protocol with a reliable **start → poll → fetch** pattern. A playbook can take several minutes, but AI tool calls are subject to short timeouts you don't control (the MCP server, the client, proxies), so trying to wait for the answer in one call is fragile. Now every call returns in seconds. **New / Improved** - **Start returns immediately.** `adjutantai_start_playbook` (the old `adjutantai_run_playbook` name is removed) hands back a run id at once with a hint on how to poll. - **Check progress** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_status` — queued, running, completed, or failed (a run that hit a recoverable error and is auto‑retrying is reported as still running, not failed), with guidance to stop polling after ~15 minutes. - **Fetch the verdict** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_results` once completed — condensed by default, or the full result on request; a partial result is clearly labelled. - **Tenant‑safe.** One team can't read another team's run; unknown or expired run ids simply return "not found." Run records are kept for 7 days by default. - **Try it out of the box:** start `MCP Example: Read-only Health Check` under Org/BU `DFLT/DFLT` (the read‑only reference playbook shipped on every install), then poll and fetch. Requires the inbound MCP server and the Backend Ask Service to be enabled. No configuration changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. ### Also in 1.8.4 — the Outcome Ledger (Enterprise) A single screen that answers what a CEO, CISO or auditor actually asks: *what did agentic AI do for us this period, was it any good, what did it save, what did it cost — and can I see the evidence for one run?* It assembles data the app already records (unattended‑run history, analyst agreement, run telemetry, LLM spend) into one executive/audit view. It adds **no new data collection and sends nothing to any external service.** **New** - **The dashboard** (`Adjutant AI ▸ Outcome Ledger`): headline tiles (investigations run without a human, how often analysts agreed with the AI — with the sample size and coverage shown, benign/false‑positive runs auto‑closed, analyst hours saved, LLM spend, typical time to a verdict), the mix of AI conclusions over time, agreement by case type, a weekly ledger, and an **evidence** table you can click through to the full detail of any single run. A footer spells out every assumption so a number is never quoted out of context. - **Safe to hand to an auditor.** What each viewer may see is decided on the server from their own identity — never from the page — and fails closed. In this release the dashboard is for Splunk administrators; scoped, delegated auditor access is the next step. - **Is the AI real, or just performing?** An Efficacy Trend panel puts run volume against how often analysts agreed, over time. If the agent runs more while analysts increasingly override it, the panel says so ("scaling faster than trust") instead of hiding it behind a healthy‑looking headline — and on too little feedback it honestly says the sample is too thin to judge. - **Honest numbers.** Effort saved is shown as time (with the per‑case assumption stated), spend is the real logged cost, and the per‑investigation efficiency signal is token usage — never an invented cost estimate. Enterprise feature. No effect on any existing behaviour. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.3 "Security hardening" A security‑focused release. Adjutant AI was put through an independent OWASP Top 10 (web **and** LLM), dependency‑vulnerability, and "AI‑driven ransomware" review. The headline: **no critical issues, no default passwords or keys, no vulnerable components that ship to you, and the assistant cannot be turned into an attack tool.** Confirmed issues are fixed; a plain‑language, reviewer‑ready write‑up ships in the app as `SECURITY_AUDIT.md`. **Improved / Fixed** - **Credentials stay server‑side.** Provider API keys and keyless Azure sign‑in secrets are never sent to the browser or to other users in your tenant. (The free‑tier browser API‑key path is unchanged.) - **Prompts stay in your audit index**, not Splunk's internal logs. - **Stronger multi‑tenant isolation** for investigation results and knowledge sources. - **You confirm every change.** Closing a notable, setting a disposition, an ITSI/TrackMe/ServiceNow write, or overwriting a saved dashboard now asks for explicit confirmation first. Read‑only questions and new private dashboards are unaffected. - **General hardening:** cleaner errors, tighter sign‑in redirects, safer content‑pack imports, email TLS verification on by default. No new features or config changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.2 "Edge Processor data-quality + keyless Azure OpenAI auth" **Keyless Azure OpenAI (Microsoft Entra ID / managed identity).** Connect Azure OpenAI **without a static API key** — using a Microsoft Entra ID service principal or a managed identity, governed by your Entra tenant. Runs entirely server-side (no token reaches the browser), supports Public and US Gov clouds, and adds a one-click **Test connection** that names exactly what to fix if something is off. Connecting Azure with a plain **API key** still works on every tier; the keyless Entra path is an **Enterprise** capability. --- ### Edge Processor data-quality If your data passes through **Splunk Edge Processor** before it reaches Splunk, some parsing, timestamping, dropping and routing happens *upstream* — where Splunk's own internal logs and feed-health tools can't see it. This release teaches the assistant to look at that hop. - **New "Edge Processor → Splunk data-quality check".** Ask the assistant to check an Edge Processor feed and it reads Edge Processor's own operational metrics (throughput, dropped events, failed destination sends, and queue backpressure) and tells you, in plain language, whether data is being silently lost or delayed before it lands — with a proof dashboard. - **Honest by design.** If Edge Processor telemetry isn't reaching your Splunk yet, the assistant says so and gives you the exact setup steps (on-premises vs Splunk Cloud) instead of inventing a clean bill of health. It reports at the pipeline level and is clear that per-event checks need a small addition to your Edge Processor pipeline. - **Folds into the readiness verdict.** Edge Processor joins Splunk parsing, feed-health, and Cribl as another "is this data actually good?" signal, and can cap the Data Quality Score when it finds upstream loss. - Read-only and available on every tier, exactly like the existing Cribl check. --- ## 1.8.1 "Cleaner support diagnosis" A small maintenance update over 1.8.0 (front-end only). - **More accurate "Report an issue" diagnosis.** The automated issue classifier no longer mislabels a session that finished normally — one that completed and produced its dashboard — as having "run out of tool steps." The suspected-issue summary in your support bundle is now cleaner for healthy, tool-heavy sessions. --- ## 1.8.0 "Agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs & all-tiers data quality" **New — your SOC can watch the agent (OCSF telemetry).** - **Adjutant AI emits its own activity as OCSF.** Every LLM call, tool / MCP / ServiceNow call, configuration change, unattended run verdict, and **policy refusal** (the proof the controls actually fire) can be written as open-standard **OCSF** events to a Splunk index your Enterprise Security / SOC already watches — mapped to CIM via the community **OCSF-CIM Add-On**. Your SOC monitors our agent the same way it monitors everything else: on-prem, with no cloud egress. - **You stay in control.** It is **off by default** and Enterprise-gated. **You provision and name the index** (the app ships no `indexes.conf`). Routing and content are resolved **per Organisation / Business Unit**; content export is denied by default and never exceeds your audit (DPIA) ceiling, with a server-side redaction check before anything is written. - **See it immediately.** A shipped admin dashboard — *Adjutant AI — Behaviour (OCSF)* — shows the token trend, model mix, tool/MCP egress with identity, the refusal and finding feeds, and a per-run drilldown, all on raw OCSF (no CIM Add-On required). **New — update Adjutant's content without waiting for a whole new app release.** - **Content packs.** Almost everything Adjutant does well lives in its **content** — the skills, knowledge, and playbooks. A **content pack** is a single, versioned file that lets us ship a corrected or improved content set straight to your install, and lets your admin apply it safely — no Splunkbase re-vetting cycle for a content fix. - **Your changes are protected.** Applying a pack **upgrades only the items you haven't changed**. Anything your team has customised is left exactly as-is and clearly listed, never silently overwritten — and your Org/BU scoping is always preserved. After an import you get a per-item report, and the list of items that need manual reconciliation is downloadable as a CSV. - **Safe by design.** Every pack carries an integrity check, so a tampered or truncated file is refused. Imports live on the **Backups** page, which also shows which content version you're currently on — run a backup first and you can roll back in one click. - **Retire without deleting.** A pack can mark an item **retired** — it stays installed but is hidden and switched off everywhere (it can't be picked, run, or used by the assistant). An admin can re-enable it at any time by removing the tag. **Improved — data-quality checks for everyone, and Splunk 10.x readiness.** - **Data-quality ingestion checks are now available on every edition, including the free tier.** Checking whether a feed is actually landing and parsing correctly — on `index=_internal`, through **TrackMe**, and through **Cribl Stream** — is a baseline capability now, not a Professional add-on. - **Ready for Splunk Enterprise 10.2 and 10.4.** The app declares Python 3.9 **and** 3.13 compatibility and has been audited against the 10.x platform changes (dashboards, the web framework, KV Store). Your admin still completes the standard KV Store engine migration as part of any 10.x upgrade. - **Smarter Dashboard Studio building.** The assistant now works from a single, version-aware map of what Dashboard Studio supports on **your** Splunk version — it won't reach for a chart type your version can't render, and when your Splunk is newer than what we've documented it builds conservatively and verifies the result. **Fixed.** - **Fewer false "the dashboard is blank" errors.** A heavy Dashboard Studio dashboard that renders fine but slowly is no longer wrongly reported as blank — the assistant confirms the panels actually returned data before deciding, so it stops wasting a retry on a dashboard that was already correct. A genuinely blank dashboard is still caught. - **TrackMe panels only when they belong.** Fixed a rule that pushed a TrackMe feed-health panel onto every generated dashboard (and used a lookup that fails outside the TrackMe app). The assistant now adds a feed-health panel only when it's actually relevant, using a method that works in your app. --- ## 1.7.0 "ServiceNow integration" (included in the 1.8.0 release) > **Renamed to Adjutant AI.** The app is now **Adjutant AI** (formerly "AI Workbench"). > This is a **display-name change only** — the in-app title (the easter egg now lives on > the dot of the "i" in **Adjutant Ai**), the app label, the documentation, and the > assistant's own self-description all say **Adjutant AI**. Nothing functional changed: > the Splunk app id, your saved searches/dashboards/models, KVStore data, and generated > artifact names are unchanged, so the upgrade is seamless. **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other Splunk apps.** - **On a schedule or on an event.** A playbook can run **unattended** on a schedule (a "morning health check") or in response to a Splunk event — an alert, an ES correlation search, or an ITSI episode. When an event triggers it, the affected thing (the host, user, or entity in the alert) is handed to the playbook automatically, so it investigates exactly what fired. Two ready-made (disabled) examples are included to copy. - **Adjutant AI as a building block for other apps.** Other Splunk AI agents can now ask Adjutant AI to **list** and **run** your playbooks through a small, safe interface (an MCP server). Only playbooks you mark **MCPready** are exposed, every call must name the Org/BU it is for (which must be a business unit you have set up) as a safeguard, and runs go through the same governed, bounded service — never an open door. This interface is **off by default** — turn it on with one setting. When on, the tools can also appear inside **Splunk's own MCP Server**, reachable on the normal Splunk web address (no special port needed); you authenticate with a standard Splunk token. A ready-made, read-only **example playbook** ships enabled so there is always something to see the moment you switch the interface on. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** - One click on any conversation (per-turn 🐞, the Ask panel, or the new **Help tab**) packages exactly what happened — versions, the resolved prompt, the tools and model used, the generated dashboards/searches, and every error and warning — into a single file. - **Safe by construction:** secrets are stripped before anything leaves the browser, and the file is **encrypted** to the support key, so it's safe to send over any channel. - It even **tells you what kind of problem it looks like** and matches known issues, so simple cases are solved without a back-and-forth. - **Send it your way:** download it and attach it to your own ticket, use the built-in support form, or email it. The **Help tab** (Report + Documentation + About) is always reachable — even if the app is locked by licensing. **New — ServiceNow, done properly** (Professional + the `servicenow` feature). Read incidents, changes, problems and the **CMDB/CSDM** in plain English — with bounded blast-radius / dependency traversals ("what's the blast radius if this CI fails?"). Turn a Splunk alert, ITSI episode or ES notable into a rich, deterministically rendered ServiceNow incident and **write the number back** to the originating object (a re-fire updates, never duplicates; the closed-incident policy is configurable). **Security incidents (SIR)** with MITRE ATT&CK, off until an admin enables them. Two transports (REST **or** a ServiceNow MCP server), plus TISC threat-intel enrichment — all server-side and allowlisted, so ServiceNow can never block the assistant. *(Verified against the documented APIs and unit-tested; final certification is on a live ServiceNow.)* **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other apps.** Playbooks can run **unattended** on a schedule, or from a Splunk alert / ES correlation search / ITSI episode (the triggering entity is handed to the run). Adjutant AI can also expose **list / run** over an inbound **MCP server** (off by default, MCPready-only, Org/BU-scoped) — reachable inside Splunk's own MCP Server on the normal web address, with a standard Splunk token. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** One click packages a failing conversation — secret-stripped and **encrypted client-side** — with an automatic problem classification, plus an always-reachable **Help tab** even when the app is licence-locked. **New — Cribl Stream data-quality awareness** (Professional+). Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Turn-level audit logging made reliable; more robust dashboard generation. - **1.4.0** — The assistant reads your own Splunk **live** (real search commands + installed visualizations) instead of guessing; Splunk Security Essentials detection content integrated. - **1.3.3** — TrackMe integration end-to-end (feed-health awareness + actions) with richer built-in platform knowledge. - **1.3.2** — First Splunkbase 1.x release: packaging and permissions hardening. - **1.3.1** — Fixed Org/BU edits dropping fields; safeguard to keep bundled playbooks correct after upgrades. - **1.3.0** — Real, per-Organisation audit logging of every AI interaction (Professional+). - **1.2.0** — Splunk Security Essentials content tools for playbooks. - **1.1.1** — Cisco Deep Time Series Model (CDTSM) playbooks: pre-trained anomaly detection and forecasting via the AI Toolkit, each with a proof dashboard. - **1.1.0** — Multi-tenancy and the Organisation / Business-Unit editor overhauled for clearer, safer tenant scoping. - **1.0.0** — The knowledge layer: ground answers in your organisation's own conventions. *(Releases before 1.0 are early pre-release history and are omitted here.)* --- ## Known issues - **Open the assistant from inside another app.** Adjutant AI is a "host shell": reach it from a navigation-menu entry inside Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI, or your own apps — not by clicking the app tile directly. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*


Short Description:
A workbench for Splunk, not just a chatbot. Analyse, correlate and build across SPL, dashboards, alerts, AI Toolkit / MLTK, ES, ITSI and TrackMe through tools that understand each one — plus any MCP server you add. Pick your LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama, OpenRouter. Multi-tenant, multi-tier (Free, Pro, Enterprise, MSP).


Description:
Adjutant AI turns the Splunk your platform team built into something the business can use. Install it on your search head and it drives the Adjutant AI Domain Workspace (app 9691, arriving on Splunkbase shortly): your saved searches, dashboards, lookups and data models assembled into a workspace people work in. Ask in plain language, comment on what you find, claim and hand over rows, and every role gets its own perspective on one model: business on one side, plumbing on the other. Every number comes from a real search run as that user, never from the model. This is how Splunk reaches the business side of IT. Underneath it is a full generative workbench: ask in English, get back working SPL, dashboards, alerts, lookups and MLTK pipelines, built against your running environment and run for real before saving. New in 2.5: your first LLM connection takes a minute instead of a week. Pick a provider, paste whatever URL you have, and the setup wizard works out the endpoint, the API version, the route, your proxy and what must bypass it, TLS interception, and whether your token ceiling can carry a question. Ten checks prove the whole path, ending in a real answer and a real Splunk tool call, because a connection that authenticates and then ignores tools looks healthy until the first question. Every failure names what happened, who can fix it and how long it takes, with a block to paste into a ticket when it belongs to another team. What the AI already in Splunk does not give you: Your keys never leave the building. Bring your own model, Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock, Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter or Ollama fully offline, running server side on your search head. It knows your Splunk, not Splunk in general. Fine grained tools across Core, ES, ITSI, TrackMe, ServiceNow and the AI Toolkit under your existing roles, with your macros expanded and syntax read live from your box. An engineer who distrusts AI can check the working. ITSI Root Cause Analysis walks your dependency graph and scores the evidence with no LLM in the analysis, so a red KPI on a dead feed is named as a data problem, and the same evidence always gives the same answer. Fraud rings a risk threshold structurally cannot find: many accounts each too small to alert, sharing a device or payout account. A coverage audit grades your estate against nine fraud use cases, AML included. Your SOC can watch the agent. LLM calls, tool calls, config changes and policy refusals go out as OCSF events to an index Enterprise Security already reads. Explain a SPL search and the fraud demo dataset are free on every tier. The workspace and most of the depth are licence gated, so a download alone shows the shape, not the substance. Come and see it properly: a free hour on video on your use cases, then a proof of value licence scoped to what you want to prove. PoV customers see the workspace before Splunkbase does, and get a real say in what it does next. eduard.lekanne@thedutchdatadifference.nl

Release Notes:
## FIXED - The Monitor status banner named a single remedy regardless of the actual cause. When a WLM admission rule filters by role, switching detection to an explicit index list cannot help. The banner now identifies which of the two remediations your environment needs, names the admission rule involved, and links to the right one. - That banner linked to "Settings" — a page renamed to Configuration in v1.15.0. The link now resolves. - If the scheduler logged detection as filtered but Workload Management reports no rule that would filter it, the Run As panel no longer reports "no action needed" over a live block. It reports that the cause could not be confirmed and offers both remediations. - On Splunk Cloud, where Workload Management endpoints are not readable, the message now names the admission rule the scheduler actually recorded instead of falling back to generic guidance. - A failed diagnosis now explains itself and points at the panel that can help, instead of showing "check permissions." ## CHANGED - The Index Scope and Run As panels now share one diagnosis per page load instead of each running its own scheduler-log search. - Links from the Monitor banner scroll directly to the relevant section of the Configuration page.


Short Description:
Know the moment a data source goes silent. Data Heartbeat monitors every source type in your Splunk environment and fires Slack, Teams, webhook, or email alerts the instant data stops flowing — before gaps turn into blind spots.


Description:
Data Heartbeat monitors your Splunk environment for source types that have stopped sending data. When a data source goes silent — whether from a misconfigured forwarder, a failed log shipper, or a broken integration — Data Heartbeat detects the gap and alerts you before the silence becomes a blind spot. Every monitored source type has a configurable threshold, measured in minutes. When no data arrives within that window, the app flags the source type and fires your chosen alert action: Slack, Microsoft Teams, a generic webhook, or email via Splunk's built-in SMTP relay. Key features: • Monitor dashboard — a live status table showing every tracked source type, the minutes since its last event, its threshold, and its importance level, with color-coded severity (green, yellow, red, and critical). • Per-row alert actions — each source type can use its own notification target, independent of the global default. • Auto Discovery — a nightly scan that surfaces new source types appearing in your environment and queues them for review. • Importance tagging — mark business-critical sources as High, Medium, or Low importance. When a high-importance source goes silent, the app raises a red-alert banner. • Settings page — configure global defaults (threshold, alert action, and notification target), enable or disable the monitoring pipeline, and test alert actions without waiting for a real outage. • Audit log — a full history of every configuration change, with timestamps and user attribution. • No index footprint — all configuration is stored in KV Store, so no custom indexes are required. Data Heartbeat is compatible with Splunk Enterprise 8.2+, Splunk Cloud Classic, and Splunk Cloud Victoria.

Release Notes:
GitHub - [https://github.com/splunk/security\_content/releases/tag/v6.6.0](https://github.com/splunk/security_content/releases/tag/v6.6.0) Release Notes - [https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/security-content-update/release-notes/6.6](https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/security-content-update/release-notes/6.6)


Description:
The Splunk ES Content Update (ESCU) app delivers pre-packaged Security Content. **Version 1.1.0** New configuration experience. The setup screen has been rebuilt with Splunk's Universal Configuration Console (UCC), replacing the legacy setup.xml page. Version 1.1.0 does not read the key stored by the old setup page, so the macaddresslookup command will report "No macadress.com API key configured" until you do this once. The key is still held in Splunk's encrypted credential store, never in a plain-text .conf file. Also in this release: * Declares python.required \= 3.13 for the search command and REST handler, for compatibility with current and upcoming Splunk versions. * Passes Splunk AppInspect cloud checks with no errors or failures. No change to the macaddresslookup command, its arguments, or the fields it adds. Existing saved searches and dashboards keep working unchanged once the API key is re-entered.


Short Description:
Add a macaddresslookup search command that enriches any event with a MAC address field: manufacturer, device type, virtualization/container signals, randomization confidence, and reserved/protocol address detection, all in one streaming SPL command.


Description:
TA-macadress adds a `macaddresslookup` search command that resolves MAC addresses to vendor, device category, virtualization, and special-use information, using the macadress.com API. Any event with a MAC address field, DHCP leases, ARP tables, wireless associations, switch port tables, asset inventories, can be enriched in place with: - Vendor and manufacturer identity, resolved against the full IEEE OUI registry (organization name, matched registry prefix, country) - Device category inference (router, switch, wireless access point, embedded device, and more) from a manually curated, source-verified dataset, not a guess - Virtualization and container detection: VMware, Hyper-V, Xen, VirtualBox, Parallels, QEMU/KVM, and Docker's default bridge convention - Special-use address classification: broadcast, IPv4/IPv6 multicast, VRRP, HSRP, STP, LACP, 802.1X, LLDP, each with its source protocol cited - Randomization signals: whether an address is locally administered or otherwise likely to be a privacy-randomized or spoofed MAC, useful for flagging anomalous device behavior in security and asset-inventory use cases This turns a raw MAC address into something you can actually search, filter, and stat on: `stats count by mac_organization`, `where mac_virtualization_platform!=""`, `where mac_potentially_randomized=1`, and so on, without leaving SPL. Lookups are batched (up to 100 addresses per API call) for efficiency on large event volumes, and the API key is stored via Splunk's encrypted storage/passwords endpoint rather than a plain-text configuration file. A free API key is available at macadress.com/signup; paid plans raise the request-rate and monthly-quota limits for larger deployments.

item.title: Picus Security Add-on for Splunk - v1.5.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Release notes - 1.5.0 **Requires Splunk 9.3 or later.** On Splunk 9.0, 9.1 or 9.2, install 1.4.9 instead - 1.5.0 cannot run on those versions. *** ## Added **Splunk 10 support.** Earlier releases could not run on Splunk 10 at all. Their bundled libraries used a Python API that was removed in Python 3.12, which broke both the configuration pages and data collection. If you are running Splunk 10 on an earlier release of this add-on, it is not collecting data and this upgrade fixes it. ## Changed **Rebuilt with the Splunk Add-on UCC framework.** This restores Splunk Cloud Platform compatibility and replaces the previous Add-on Builder based configuration UI. Functionally the add-on collects the same data from the same Picus API endpoints. The package is also considerably smaller - roughly 1.8 MB instead of 5.8 MB - because it no longer bundles unused libraries, and it now contains no platform-specific compiled files, so the same package installs cleanly on Linux, Windows and macOS. The add-on now opens on the **Configuration** page instead of **Inputs**, which matches the order you configure it in: an account first, then an input. ## Fixed Includes the certificate path fix from 1.4.9: data collection failing on Splunk instances not installed under `/opt/splunk`, which affected all Windows installations. ## Upgrading Install over your existing version and restart Splunk. Your accounts, inputs, stored refresh tokens and collection checkpoints are preserved, and sourcetypes are unchanged, so existing searches and dashboards keep working. No reconfiguration is needed. Two notes: * Because the add-on's internal layout changed, files from the previous release that are no longer part of it remain on disk after the upgrade. They are inert and can be left alone. If you want to remove them, back up the app's `local/` directory first - it holds your accounts, inputs and encrypted tokens - and do not simply delete and reinstall the app. * Account names must start with a letter and contain only letters, digits and underscores. This has always been the rule in the UI, but it is now enforced when saving through the API as well. An existing account whose name does not match still works and still collects data; it just cannot be edited. To change one, delete it and recreate it with a conforming name. ## Requirements * Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud Platform 9.3 or later. * Network access from the Splunk instance running the input to the Picus API over HTTPS. * A Picus API refresh token (Settings -> Rest API Token in the Picus Platform). ## Support Questions: support@picussecurity.com
